content: Post-dural puncture headache (PDPH) is a frequent complication following lumbar punctures. The condition is thought to result from cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leakage through the puncture site in the dura mater. Preventive strategies are therefore essential to mitigate this complication. While prolonged bed rest has been traditionally used as a treatment for PDPH after its onset, its effectiveness in preventing PDPH remains uncertain. Similarly, the potential benefit of administering additional fluids beyond normal dietary intake to compensate for CSF loss caused by the puncture is also unclear. The objective of this review was to evaluate whether prolonged bed rest, specific body and head positions, or supplementary fluid administration after lumbar puncture could prevent the development of PDPH in individuals undergoing the procedure for diagnostic or therapeutic purposes. The review included randomized controlled trials that compared various interventions: bed rest versus immediate mobilization, head-down tilt versus horizontal positioning, prone versus supine positions during bed rest, and supplementary fluid administration versus no or reduced fluid supplementation. The search for relevant studies was conducted across multiple databases and trial registries up to February 2015. A total of 24 trials involving 2,996 participants were included in this updated review. The sample sizes of the individual studies ranged from 39 to 382 participants. Most studies focused on comparing bed rest with immediate mobilization, while only two trials examined the effects of supplementary fluids. The overall risk of bias in the included studies was judged to be low to unclear, and the quality of evidence was rated as low to moderate due to methodological limitations. The primary outcome assessed was the occurrence of PDPH. Low-quality evidence indicated no significant benefit of bed rest compared to immediate mobilization in reducing the incidence of severe PDPH (risk ratio [RR] 0.98; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.68 to 1.41; 1,568 participants; 9 studies). Moderate-quality evidence suggested that bed rest might increase the likelihood of any headache after lumbar puncture (RR 1.16; 95% CI 1.02 to 1.32; 2,477 participants; 18 studies). Furthermore, bed rest was associated with a probable increase in PDPH incidence compared to immediate mobilization (RR 1.24; 95% CI 1.04 to 1.48; 1,519 participants; 12 studies). These findings were consistent even when the analysis was restricted to trials with low risk of bias. Regarding fluid supplementation, low-quality evidence showed no clear benefit in reducing the incidence of severe PDPH (RR 0.67; 95% CI 0.26 to 1.73; 100 participants; 1 study) or PDPH overall (RR 1.00; 95% CI 0.59 to 1.69; 100 participants; 1 study). Moderate-quality evidence suggested no significant effect on the incidence of any headache after lumbar puncture (RR 0.94; 95% CI 0.66 to 1.34; 200 participants; 2 studies). Adverse events related to these interventions were not anticipated and were not assessed in this review. In conclusion, the updated review, which included one additional study since the previous version, did not alter the overall findings. The evidence quality for most outcomes was low to moderate, primarily due to limitations in randomization and blinding in the included studies. There is no evidence to support the routine use of bed rest after dural puncture for preventing PDPH. The role of fluid supplementation in PDPH prevention remains uncertain.
